query: For single-phase ZrB2 ceramic, which requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and may lack the strength and structural integrity needed for service, what single intervention could lower the required preparation temperature and reduce the holes and eventual component failure caused by prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention and its mechanism, predict its performance compared with conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2, define the relevant preparation and service boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and describe a controlled preparation, integrity, and long-duration exposure experiment that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Utilizing spark plasma sintering (SPS) for single-phase ZrB2 will allow densification at lower temperatures, thereby reducing the formation of pores that lead to failure under prolonged liquid plating exposure.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional single-phase ZrB2 produced via high-temperature (>2300 °C) sintering with a microstructure prone to porosity and associated weakness during service.
generation.intervention: Replace the conventional high-temperature sintering process with optimized SPS processing at reduced temperatures (e.g., around 1900–2100 °C).
generation.conditions: Preparation by SPS under controlled heating rate and pulsed current settings at lower sintering temperatures; service exposure includes prolonged immersion in a liquid plating bath.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced densification and reduced porosity due to rapid heating and transient high local temperatures enabled by SPS.
generation.mechanism: The pulsed electrical current in SPS generates localized hotspots and enhanced diffusion, which promotes rapid consolidation and grain boundary healing. This results in fewer processing-induced defects and a structurally robust ceramic that is less susceptible to the formation of holes during service.
generation.predicted_outcome: SPS-processed ZrB2 will exhibit equivalent or improved mechanical strength and structural integrity compared with conventionally sintered ZrB2, with significantly reduced porosity and fewer instances of hole formation during long-duration liquid plating exposure.
generation.baseline: The conventional preparation route requires temperatures above 2300 °C, resulting in higher porosity and structural defects that lead to premature failure under liquid plating conditions.
generation.boundary: Preparation boundary: sintering temperature >2300 °C for conventional methods versus 1900–2100 °C using SPS. Service boundary: extended exposure to a liquid plating bath simulating actual operational conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal SPS parameters for ZrB2 have not been fully established, and variations in electric pulse conditions or sintering duration may lead to unpredictable microstructural features. Additionally, scaling from laboratory SPS experiments to industrial-scale processing may introduce uncertainties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of ZrB2 samples: one using conventional high-temperature sintering (>2300 °C) and one using SPS at reduced temperatures (1900–2100 °C). Characterize both sample sets for density, porosity, microstructure (via SEM), and mechanical strength. Then, expose both sets to a standardized prolonged immersion test in a liquid plating bath. Monitor for the formation and evolution of holes, measure mechanical degradation (e.g., flexural strength, fracture toughness), and compare performance.
measurements: Density and porosity (via Archimedes' method and image analysis)
Grain size and microstructural uniformity (via SEM)
Mechanical properties (e.g., flexural strength, fracture toughness)
Extent and progression of porosity/hole formation after liquid plating exposure (via periodic SEM and metallographic analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SPS-prepared ZrB2 samples do not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in densification (i.e., lower porosity), mechanical strength, and reduced hole formation during the plating bath exposure compared to the conventionally prepared samples, then the hypothesis that SPS lowers preparation temperature and enhances service durability is falsified.

Co-Cr-Fe-Mn-Ni Oxide as a Highly Efficient Thermoelectric High-Entropy Alloy

Abstract: Among the existing materials for heat conversion, high-entropy alloys are of great interest due to the tunability of their functional properties. Here, we aim to produce single-phase high-entropy oxides composed of Co-Cr-Fe-Mn-Ni-O through spark plasma sintering (SPS), testing their thermoelectric (TE) properties. This material was successfully obtained before via a different technique, which requires a very long processing time. Hence, the main target of this work is to apply spark plasma sintering, a much faster and scalable process. The samples were sintered in the temperature range of 1200–1300 °C. Two main phases were formed: rock salt-structured Fm3̅m and spinel-structured Fd3̅m. Comparable transport properties were achieved via the new approach: the highest value of the Seebeck coefficient reached −112.6 μV/K at room temperature, compared to −150 μV/K reported before; electrical properties at high temperatures are close to the properties of the single-phase material (σ = 0.2148 S/cm, σ ≈ 0.2009 S/cm reported before).
